traduccion.en: to switch from usted to tú

nota.en: Literally “to pass from usted to tú”.

explicacion.en: Nos means “each other”, so the verb must be the nosotros form: tuteamos. The yo form tuteo does not agree with nos.
Está is the usted form. Once you switch to tú, the verb changes too: ¿Cómo estás? Never mix tú with an usted verb.
Tu and tienes go together. Tiene belongs to usted, and the possessive with usted is su: ¿Tiene su cuaderno?

texto.en: In Ecuador usted is the safe choice with a boss, a client, an official or an older person. After a while, coworkers often switch to tú. The verb for this is tutear (to address someone as tú), and the habit is called el tuteo. The switch is usually proposed by the older person or the one with higher rank, while the younger or more junior person waits to be invited. You can say: ¿Nos tuteamos? (Shall we use tú with each other?), ¿Te puedo tutear? (May I use tú with you?) or Puedes tutearme (You can use tú with me). You accept with Claro, con gusto. Nos here means “each other”, as in nos vemos.

titulo.en: What changes when you use tú

texto.en: Once you use tú, every form that went with usted changes: the verb (¿Cómo está? becomes ¿Cómo estás?), the possessive (su cuaderno becomes tu cuaderno) and the pronoun (le becomes te). The word usted disappears. Do not mix the two systems: ¿Cómo está tú? is wrong because está is an usted form. Keep usted with clients, with official paperwork and with older people who have not offered tú.

titulo.en: Just a little while, a little coffee

objetivo.en: Use diminutives to soften a request or warm up the tone with a friend, and choose a neutral register in a formal message.

traduccion.en: the little while

nota.en: From el rato (the while). Say “rah-TEE-toh”: the first r is trilled. Un ratito is a friendly way to ask for a few minutes.

traduccion.en: the (little) coffee

nota.en: From el café. Say “kah-feh-SEE-toh”. Offering un cafecito is a warm, everyday gesture.

traduccion.en: the little moment

nota.en: From el momento. Common in speech; in a formal message use un momento.

traduccion.en: the little favor

nota.en: From el favor. Say “fah-bohr-SEE-toh”. It makes a request sound lighter.

traduccion.en: the little house

nota.en: From la casa. The diminutive keeps the gender: la casa → la casita.

traduccion.en: the little bread, the bread roll

nota.en: From el pan. Say “pahn-SEE-toh”.

traduccion.en: right now, in a moment

nota.en: From ahora. Say “ah-oh-REE-tah”: h is silent and the single r is a quick tap, like tt in “butter”. Depending on the context it means “right now” or “in a little while”.

traduccion.en: a little bit

nota.en: From poco. Say “poh-KEE-toh”: qu sounds like k.

traduccion.en: the little minute

nota.en: From el minuto. Say “mee-noo-TEE-toh”.

explicacion.en: Rato ends in -o, so you drop the o and add -ito: ratito, not ratoito. The ending -cito is only for words that end in -e, -n, -r or a stressed vowel.
Pan ends in -n, so the diminutive takes -cito: pancito. Do not invent other endings such as -eito.
Café ends in a stressed vowel, so it takes -cito and keeps its full form: cafecito, not cafeito.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Estimada señora: le pido un momentito de su tiempo.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Estimada señora: le pido un momento de su tiempo.

explicacion.en: In a formal message the diminutive sounds too familiar. Use the neutral form: un momento.

texto.en: Diminutives end in -ito or -ita. They can mean “small”, but in daily speech they mostly soften a request or add warmth: ¿Me das un ratito? sounds friendlier than ¿Me das un rato? They are very common in Ecuador and across Latin America. The diminutive keeps the gender of the word: la casa becomes la casita. Words ending in -o or -a drop that vowel and add -ito or -ita: rato → ratito, casa → casita, ahora → ahorita. In poco → poquito, the c becomes qu to keep the k sound.

titulo.en: Words that take -cito, and when not to use diminutives

texto.en: Words that end in -e, in -n, in -r or in a stressed vowel take -cito or -cita: café → cafecito, pan → pancito, favor → favorcito. Diminutives work best with time (ratito, minutito, ahorita), small favors and food or drink. With friends, as with Daniela, they are natural: ¿Te pido un favorcito? With your boss they are common in conversation, but in a formal message (to a bank or a government office) choose the neutral register: un momento, not un momentito.

explicacion.en: He must be followed by the participle (comido), not by the simple past. In Latin America you say hoy comí, with no he.
With a finished time such as ayer, Spain and Latin America both use the simple past: llamé. The perfect is for “today”, “this week”, “this year” in Spain.

explicacion.en: The participle of ver is irregular: visto. English speakers often make it regular, like vido.
The participle of escribir is irregular: escrito, not escribido.

titulo.en: Two ways to talk about today

texto.en: Spanish has two habits for talking about a period that is not over yet, such as hoy, esta mañana, esta semana or este año. In Spain people use the present perfect: Hoy he comido en la facultad. Esta mañana he tenido clase. In Latin America, including Ecuador, people normally use the simple past: Hoy comí en la facultad. Esta mañana tuve clase. Both forms are understood everywhere. In this course you produce the Latin American form and you recognize the Spain form, because Daniela will use it in her calls from Madrid.

With a time that is clearly over (ayer, anoche, el año pasado) Spain and Latin America agree: both use the simple past. Ayer llamé a Daniela. The perfect is formed as you already know: he, has, ha, hemos, han + participle (comido, tenido, conocido). Irregular participles stay irregular: escrito, visto. A tip for words that differ: in Spain la merienda is an afternoon snack, but in Ecuador it is the evening meal.

contexto.en: A video call between Emma (in Quito) and Daniela (in Madrid, in the first week of her master's). Daniela talks the way people do in Spain; Emma answers the way people do in Ecuador.

objetivo.en: Express disagreement politely in a meeting using «no estoy de acuerdo con que» + subjunctive, and propose another option.

traduccion.en: to disagree, to differ

nota.en: Say “dees-kreh-PAHR”. Discrepo, discrepas, discrepa.

traduccion.en: the objection

nota.en: Say “ohb-heh-SYOHN”: j sounds like a strong h.

traduccion.en: the disagreement

nota.en: Say “deh-sah-KWEHR-doh”. The opposite is el acuerdo.

traduccion.en: the high season

nota.en: Literally “the high season”: the months with the most tourists.

traduccion.en: the consensus

nota.en: Say “kohn-SEHN-soh”. Decidir por consenso means to decide by general agreement.

traduccion.en: the reconciliation (of work and other commitments)

nota.en: Say “kohn-see-lyah-SYOHN”. It is used for combining two commitments, as in la conciliación entre el trabajo y la familia (work-life balance). In legal settings it also means settling a dispute.

traduccion.en: the opinion

nota.en: Say “oh-pee-NYOHN”. Stress the last syllable.

traduccion.en: to respect

nota.en: Respeto tu opinión (tú) or respeto su opinión (usted).

traduccion.en: to agree

nota.en: Estoy de acuerdo, estás de acuerdo… Acuerdo here means “agreement”.

traduccion.en: to raise, to put forward

nota.en: Say “plahn-teh-AHR”. Plantear una objeción means to raise an objection.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: No estoy de acuerdo con que hacemos el taller en diciembre.

explicacion.en: After no estoy de acuerdo con que the verb goes in the subjunctive: hagamos, not hacemos. English has no such change, so the indicative feels natural.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: No estoy de acuerdo que hagamos el taller en diciembre.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: No estoy de acuerdo con que hagamos el taller en diciembre.

explicacion.en: English says “I don't agree that…” with no preposition, but Spanish needs con: no estoy de acuerdo con que.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Me parece que la propuesta sea buena.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Me parece que la propuesta es buena.

explicacion.en: Me parece que is followed by the indicative when you give an opinion: es buena. The subjunctive comes after no estoy de acuerdo con que.
After ¿Y si…? use the ordinary present: hacemos. Do not use the subjunctive here.

texto.en: To say you disagree with a plan, Spanish uses no estoy de acuerdo con que + subjunctive: No estoy de acuerdo con que hagamos el taller en diciembre. The idea after con que is a proposal or an evaluation, not a fact you state, so the verb is in the subjunctive. Agreeing works the same way: Estoy de acuerdo con que sea en febrero. Keep con before que: English says “I don't agree that…”, but Spanish needs no estoy de acuerdo con que. By contrast, to give an opinion you use me parece que + indicative: Me parece que la propuesta es buena.

titulo.en: Soften it, then propose something else

texto.en: In a meeting, disagreement sounds polite when you open with a softener: Entiendo, pero… or Respeto tu opinión, pero… (with usted: Respeto su opinión, pero…). Then offer another option with ¿Y si…? and the ordinary present: ¿Y si lo hacemos en febrero? If you plan to raise a point in a meeting, you can say you want to plantear una objeción. Be careful with the verb forms, which you already know: hagamos (hacer), sea (ser), empecemos (empezar).

contexto.en: A meeting at Andes Vivos with Inés Cárdenas (the director), Emma and Andrés Vaca (from the institute), who will give an English workshop for the guides. Emma uses usted with Inés and tú with Andrés.

dialogo.texto: Buenos días. Hoy tenemos que decidir la fecha del taller de inglés para los guías. Yo propongo hacerlo en diciembre.

traduccion.en: Good morning. Today we have to decide the date of the English workshop for the guides. I propose doing it in December.

dialogo.texto: Para mí, diciembre es posible.

traduccion.en: For me, December is possible.

dialogo.texto: Entiendo, pero no estoy de acuerdo con que lo hagamos en diciembre, porque los guías están ocupados con la temporada alta.

traduccion.en: I understand, but I don't agree that we do it in December, because the guides are busy with the high season.

dialogo.texto: Es verdad. Los guías trabajan mucho en diciembre. ¿Qué propones?

traduccion.en: That's true. The guides work a lot in December. What do you suggest?

dialogo.texto: Quiero plantear otra opción: ¿y si lo hacemos en febrero? En febrero hay menos turistas. Además, así tenemos tiempo para preparar el programa.

traduccion.en: I want to put forward another option: what if we do it in February? In February there are fewer tourists. Also, that way we have time to prepare the program.

dialogo.texto: Estoy de acuerdo con que sea en febrero. Para mí lo importante es la conciliación entre el trabajo y el taller: los guías pueden trabajar con los turistas y después ir al taller.

traduccion.en: I agree that it should be in February. For me the important thing is reconciling work and the workshop: the guides can work with the tourists and then go to the workshop.

dialogo.texto: Respeto tu opinión, Emma, y me parece que tienes razón. ¿Alguien tiene alguna objeción?

traduccion.en: I respect your opinion, Emma, and I think you are right. Does anyone have an objection?

dialogo.texto: Yo no. Para mí febrero está bien.

traduccion.en: Not me. For me February is fine.

dialogo.texto: Yo tampoco. Gracias, Andrés.

traduccion.en: Neither do I. Thank you, Andrés.

dialogo.texto: Entonces lo decidimos por consenso: el taller es en febrero. Gracias a los dos.

traduccion.en: Then we decide by consensus: the workshop is in February. Thank you both.

dialogo.texto: Gracias a usted, Inés.

traduccion.en: Thank you, Inés.

traduccion.en: to assign

explicacion.en: To assign a task, que is followed by the subjunctive: confirme, not confirma. The indicative would only describe what Andrés does.
With que + subjunctive the pronouns go before the verb and stay separate: que me lo envíen. They are attached to the verb only in affirmative commands (Envíamelo).
Encargarse always takes de: se encarga de, and de + el becomes del.

texto.en: To hand a task to someone else, Spanish starts with que and uses the subjunctive: Que lo haga Andrés (Let Andrés do it). Que Emma prepare el programa. It works like an order or a wish that someone else carries out. The subject can come before the verb or after it: Que Andrés confirme la sala. Que confirme Andrés la sala. To ask who is responsible, use ¿quién se encarga de…? and answer Yo me encargo de… or Se encarga Inés.

Object pronouns go before the verb and stay separate: Que lo haga Andrés. Que me lo envíen hoy. Que se lo diga Inés. In se lo, the pronoun se replaces le: Que se lo diga Inés means Let Inés tell it to him, to her or to them. A deadline can be added with dentro de + time: Lo necesito dentro de dos días. You will also see dentro de dos semanas in the meeting.
